newsitem.title: PERU: Lima hostage crisis hits three-month milestone.
newsitem.headline: Lima hostage crisis hits three-month milestone.

text.p: The Lima hostage crisis reached its three-month milestone on Monday with prospects still distant for an end to the grueling ordeal for 72 dignitaries held under the gun by Peru's Marxist rebels.

In a short speech on the 90th day of the siege, President Alberto Fujimori had little to offer his country beyond lamenting the captives' plight as a "terrible situation." Families of the hostages holed up in the besieged Japanese ambassador's residence began a day of solidarity, including a nationwide demonstration.

"All Peruvians, when the clocks strike midday, should sound any object as a show of solidarity with our families who have been deprived of their liberty for three months," said one relative, who asked not to be named. Churches were to chime bells, motorists to sound horns and others to whistle or bang pots and pans in the streets.
An open letter from the families described the time since the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) takeover of the diplomatic compound as "three months of agony and suffering."

More than 500 hostages were taken on Dec. 17 when some 20 jungle-trained rebels blew a hole in the residence's outer wall, swarmed into the building in a fierce shootout and took control. But the MRTA gradually released most of its prisoners, keeping those it considered most valuable as bargaining chips in its central aim of freeing some 400 jailed comrades.

The remaining captives -- a glittering list of top diplomats, security chiefs, ministers, judges and businessmen -- are mainly middle-aged and increasingly ailing, intelligence and medical reports say. Stress, gum diseases and skin ailments are common.

The hostages have already passed Christmas and New Year inside the cramped building with the windows closed and no air conditioning despite the hot Lima summer. They look likely to spend Easter there, too.

"The basic problem is now almost the same as 90 days ago -- how to deal with the demand for freedom of MRTA prisoners. No political way to deal with this has yet been found," former captive and opposition legislator Javier Diez Canseco, released in the early days of the crisis, told Reuters.
"I think of the hostages every day, of what they are going through," he added.

Bolivian Foreign Minister Antonio Aranibar sent a greeting to his country's ambassador and hostage, Jorge Gumucio, who was involved in a recent flare-up with the MRTA inside the home. Local television reported Gumucio had "an attack of hysteria" and calmed down only after being shouted at by a rebel.
"I want to salute the behaviour of Ambassador Gumucio, my friend, a great man for handling such a difficult situation with strength and serenity," Aranibar told local radio by telephone from La Paz.

He said the three-month milestone should be used as a time for reflection. "Ninety days is too much. However, there is no short-term solution in sight, as the two peoples (of Peru and Bolivia) demand," he added.

The only activity at the siege site early on Monday was the now routine singing at dawn of revolutionary anthems by the MRTA. This was quickly drowned out by police blaring tropical dance music from huge loudspeakers aimed at the residence.

Members of a three-man guarantors commission overseeing negotiations between the government and rebels were expected to meet on Monday with MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa and his second-in-command Rolly Rojas, local radio said.

The guarantors are meeting separately with the MRTA and government negotiator Domingo Palermo in an effort to pave the way for a negotiated solution after 10 rounds of face-to-face talks apparently brought little more than a polite exchange of divergent positions.

Pollster Apoyo S.A. released a survey showing that more than half of Peruvians believe the crisis -- Latin America's longest hostage siege -- will take at least one month more to resolve. Thirty-three percent of those surveyed believed the crisis would last another one to three months, while 20 percent thought it would take more than three months.

With the negotiation process crawling along, Tokyo sent Vice Foreign Minister Masahiko Komura to Peru on Monday on a week-long mission to help promote a solution. Komura was also due to visit Cuba and the Dominican Republic, both of which have offered asylum to the MRTA if an agreement is reached.
